results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 65 aligned paragraph summaries match the controlling ideas of their spec paragraphs, in the spec's order; the five intro callouts carry the KEY POINTS thesis and roadmap and match no spec paragraph, as expected.

Scene ¶4 was outlined with two ideas, but its cost figures and familiar action items set up Ingrid's different question as one contrast, which is the spec's single controlling idea (p08). The other two-idea units are listed as separate failures.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶6
results.quote: OLX is reported to have published a two-part post in 2021 on load shedding with NGINX using adaptive concurrency control; it could not be retrieved or verified for this book, so treat it as a pointer, not evidence.
results.finding: The paragraph's rules for retries, timeouts and admission control are followed by a separate idea, a note on the verification status of an OLX post. The outliner needed two summaries, and flow reader A called it a distracting aside. The spec only requires the pointer to be marked as unverified. One short attributive clause tied to the admission-control sentence would keep a single controlling idea.

results.quote: It also answers the part's opening test:
results.finding: The paragraph first recaps Part VII's platform and contracts, then adds the answer to the part's opening test with 'also'. The outliner read these as two ideas. The spec's controlling idea is that the contracts, owners and checks are what answer the test ('which answers'). The answer should be shown as the consequence of the contracts, not as a second point added on.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: the scene and traffic to S1, the journeys and incident severity to S2, control points and capacity to S3, degradation and regions to S4, the edge and AI-crawler paragraphs to S5, cost to S6. The judging sections apply S1 to S6, and the conclusion synthesizes S2, S3, S4 and S6.

Each figure caption states what the figure shows. Each table is framed or followed by a reading: traffic ('three of them can be predicted'), journeys (the three design choices), control layers ('No single control stops it, so control is layered'), caches (the two lessons), ladder, regions, cost (three readings), worked example (p49), trade-offs (p51) and verticals (p53). Quotations and statistics (SRE, Vinted, Imperva, Rightmove, AWS, Adevinta, FinOps, Cloudflare) are each followed or preceded by what they show.

results.draft_locus: Multiple Regions: How Far to Go ¶3
results.quote: For a country-scoped classifieds group the right answer for most journeys is **multi-zone plus a tested read-only mode**.
results.finding: The declared relationship is cause_effect, carrying over 'regional failure and its lessons' (the AWS event: shared control planes fail together, autoscaling is not capacity). The opening sentence follows the options table and states the recommendation without saying that it follows from those lessons. The causal link at the boundary is left implicit.

The declared relationship is contrast, carrying over 'trade-offs that hold for every vertical' and introducing where the verticals differ. 'too' signals addition, not contrast, and the sentence does not pick up the trade-offs. Flow reader A named this the weakest link between sections.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶1
results.quote: keep batch work out of peak windows with the peak calendar set out under capacity planning
results.finding: 'Peak and campaign calendar' is on audience.does_not_know. Here and in the Figure 3 caption ('by the same calendar') it is used three sections before Capacity Planning defines it. A short gloss at first use (a shared calendar of campaigns, sends, imports and batch jobs) would give the term before relying on it, and the spec order can stay.
results.corroborated_by: Both flow readers reported this: flow reader A, item 3 ('uses the calendar before it is explained, and Figure 3's caption depends on it too'); flow reader B, item 3 ('This forward reference made me stop. The calendar is used here before it is introduced.'). The term is also on does_not_know.

results.finding: Both readers stopped at this forward reference. Flow reader A: 'uses the calendar before it is explained'. The spec order (control points before capacity) is sound. The difficulty comes from naming the calendar without saying what it is.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: Control Points in the Search Path ¶6
results.quote: OLX is reported to have published a two-part post in 2021 on load shedding with NGINX using adaptive concurrency control; it could not be retrieved or verified for this book, so treat it as a pointer, not evidence.
results.finding: Flow reader A: 'This is a distracting aside.' The verification caveat breaks the run of marketplace retry rules.

The introduction opens with a direct statement placing the chapter in Part VII and states its stance: reliability is knowing the traffic shape. It then gives the asymmetric stakes, the neighbours and a roadmap. It is not a placeholder, a restated question, a dictionary definition, a 'dawn of man' opening or a book report.

The conclusion does not open with 'in conclusion' and does not merely restate the thesis. The Part VII closing and the Part VIII hand-off are required by the spec and AC-4. It holds no body evidence and is not a grab bag.

¶1 states what no single section states: one piece of knowledge, which journeys make liquidity and when, sets the objectives, calendar, ladder order and unit costs. ¶2 synthesizes Part VII as contracts with owners and checks. ¶3 gives the so-what: building those contracts across an acquired group is a problem of change for Part VIII.

¶1 returns to Ingrid's question from the scene ('Ingrid asked why nothing knew that Sunday at 20:35 mattered'). ¶2 answers the part introduction's opening test for the Rotterdam city bike, with the listing-gone objective as the check.

The cold reader recovered the brown-out frame and every section in roadmap order: traffic with bots, journey SLOs, control points with edge bot controls, capacity, degradation, regions, incidents, cost, the rerun, trade-offs, verticals, failure modes, the CA view, questions and the Part VII close. It also named the evidence (SRE, Vinted, Adevinta, Rightmove, FinOps, bot reports, fictional Veldmark) and the tone (declarative, practical, business-framed).

results.draft_locus: Cost: Making Scale Visible per Unit of Work ¶3
results.quote: And **about a third of Tradeyard's search cost serves automated clients**, most of which bring no buyers.
results.finding: The cold reader's answer covers six of the seven expected elements: a human-counted search SLO with a separate peak window and a change-gating budget policy; a calendar marketing joins that blocks batch work; the ladder (bots, optional features, cache/freshness, browse); a gateway retry budget with jitter; and edge bot classification. It omits 'cost per thousand human searches reported per owner'. The chapter never ties unit costs to the brown-out's remedy: the review's accepted actions and the rerun are reliability-only, and this reading of the cost baseline stops at a general cost decision. The cost reading could connect the automated third that amplified the brown-out to cost per thousand human searches reported per brand owner.

The last section states what the eight chapters share: a published contract (from the listing event to the journey objective), an owner and a check. It says this matters for Part VIII because building them across acquired brands and old teams is a problem of change. It answers the part's opening test explicitly for the Rotterdam city bike.
